title: Serum Protein Electrophoresis: Monoclonal Spike or Polyclonal Rise?
summary: Watch serum proteins separate into five zones, see one plasma-cell clone raise a narrow spike while inflammation raises a broad hump, and confirm the culprit with immunofixation — on serum, not plasma.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 20 Hit 1 (core: SPEP screens for monoclonal gammopathies), Hit 2 (fractions and their proteins), Trap 1 (fibrinogen pseudo-spike in plasma) and the Figure 20 memory anchor. Checked against O’Connell 2005, the European Myeloma Network 2018 recommendations and Winter & Bertholf 2012 (ADLM).

objectives: Name the five SPEP fractions in order and their main proteins.
Distinguish a monoclonal spike from a polyclonal increase and explain why each looks the way it does.
Confirm an M-protein with immunofixation, add free light chains, and recognize the fibrinogen pseudo-spike.

scenes.title: A spike in the gamma zone
scenes.altText: A protein electrophoresis tracing. Most of it looks familiar, but the gamma region shows a tall, narrow spike instead of a low, broad hump. Question tokens: “One clone of plasma cells?” and “Or just inflammation?”.

cues.text: A serum protein electrophoresis shows a tall, narrow spike in the gamma region.
Is this one clone of plasma cells making a single antibody — a monoclonal gammopathy? Or a broad reaction to inflammation?
The shape of the gamma region, and one follow-up test, answer that.

scenes.title: Normal: five zones
scenes.altText: Serum proteins migrate in an electric field from the cathode (−) toward the anode (+). Five zones appear in order from the anode: albumin (the largest peak, nearest the positive electrode), α1 (α1-antitrypsin), α2 (haptoglobin, α2-macroglobulin, ceruloplasmin), β (transferrin, β-lipoprotein, complement C3) and γ (immunoglobulins), with a normal γ region a low, broad hump.

cues.text: In serum protein electrophoresis, proteins move through a gel or capillary in an electric field. Albumin forms the largest peak, closest to the positive electrode.
Next come the alpha-one zone, mostly alpha-one antitrypsin, and the alpha-two zone: haptoglobin, alpha-two macroglobulin and ceruloplasmin.
Then the beta zone, with transferrin, beta-lipoprotein and complement C3.
Finally the gamma zone, nearest the negative electrode, where the immunoglobulins run. Normally it is a low, broad hump, because many different plasma cells each make a slightly different antibody.

scenes.title: What changes: monoclonal vs polyclonal
scenes.altText: Two γ regions side by side. Left: one clone of plasma cells produces identical antibody molecules, which migrate together as a narrow, tall spike (M-protein), often with the rest of the γ region lower than normal. Right: many clones respond to inflammation, infection or liver disease, giving a broad, diffuse rise across the γ region (polyclonal gammopathy).

cues.text: If one clone of plasma cells expands, every antibody it makes is identical. Identical molecules migrate together, so they form a narrow, tall spike: a monoclonal, or M, protein.
The spike often sits on a gamma region that is otherwise lower than normal, as the clone crowds out normal antibody production.

In inflammation, chronic infection or liver disease such as cirrhosis, many different clones respond. Their antibodies differ slightly, so they spread out into a broad, diffuse rise: a polyclonal gammopathy.
Narrow spike: think monoclonal. Broad hump: think polyclonal and reactive. Screening for monoclonal gammopathies is the main reason labs run this test.

props.label: Main use of SPEP: screening for monoclonal gammopathies

scenes.title: In the lab: confirm and type the spike
scenes.altText: A suspected spike leads to immunofixation (IFE): lanes for IgG, IgA, IgM, κ and λ; a band appears in one heavy-chain lane and one light-chain lane (e.g. IgG κ). Notes: IFE is about ten times more sensitive than SPEP and is required at diagnosis to type the M-protein; SPEP quantifies the spike for follow-up. Light-chain-only disease can be missed by SPEP and IFE, so a serum free light-chain assay is added; the myeloma work-up includes SPEP with IFE, serum free light chains and a 24-hour urine.

cues.text: A spike needs confirming and typing. Immunofixation runs the sample in lanes treated with antibodies against IgG, IgA, IgM, kappa and lambda.
A true M-protein shows one heavy chain and one light chain — for example IgG kappa.
Immunofixation is about ten times more sensitive than electrophoresis and is needed at diagnosis. Electrophoresis then measures the size of the spike over time.
Some myelomas make only light chains, which are small and quickly cleared by the kidneys. Electrophoresis and immunofixation can miss them, so a serum free light-chain test is added.
The initial work-up for myeloma combines electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains and a 24-hour urine collection.

props.label: IFE ≈ 10× more sensitive · types the spike
SPEP measures the spike over time
Light-chain-only disease can be missed → serum free light chains
Myeloma work-up: SPEP + IFE · serum free light chains · 24-h urine

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Narrow band between β and γ = monoclonal gammopathy” is crossed out → “Check the tube: plasma (fibrinogen) makes a pseudo-spike; immunofixation is negative. Repeat on serum.” Trap card: “Normal SPEP rules out myeloma” is crossed out → “Small or light-chain-only M-proteins can be missed: immunofixation and free light chains.”

cues.text: Trap one: a narrow band between beta and gamma isn’t automatically an M-protein. If plasma was run instead of serum, fibrinogen makes a pseudo-spike — and immunofixation is negative. Repeat on serum.
Trap two: a normal electrophoresis doesn’t rule out myeloma. Small M-proteins and light-chain-only disease can be missed; immunofixation and free light chains catch more.
And a broad gamma rise is reactive until proven otherwise — think inflammation, infection or liver disease.

props.title: ✗ “Narrow β–γ band = M-protein.”
lines: ✓ Plasma → fibrinogen pseudo-spike; IFE negative; repeat on serum

props.title: ✗ “Normal SPEP rules out myeloma.”
lines: ✓ Add immunofixation and serum free light chains

scenes.title: A choir or a soloist
scenes.altText: Memory aid: the γ region is a choir. Many voices (clones) singing slightly different notes make a broad hum — polyclonal. One soloist singing one note very loudly is a sharp spike — monoclonal — and the rest of the choir often goes quiet. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the gamma region is a choir. Many voices singing slightly different notes make a broad hum — polyclonal. One soloist belting a single note makes a spike — monoclonal — and the choir often goes quiet.

Where it breaks: an M-protein can run in the beta or even alpha-two region, some are too small to see, light chains may slip into the urine, and pseudo-spikes like fibrinogen exist. Immunofixation decides.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: M-proteins can run outside γ · small ones hide · light chains slip to urine

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Albumin → α1 → α2 → β → γ”, “Narrow spike = monoclonal · broad rise = polyclonal”, “Confirm with immunofixation; serum, not plasma”.

cues.text: Serum protein electrophoresis screens for monoclonal gammopathies: a narrow spike suggests one clone, a broad rise suggests a reactive polyclonal response, and immunofixation on serum confirms and types the protein.

props.label: Narrow spike = monoclonal · broad rise = polyclonal
Confirm with immunofixation · use serum, not plasma

explanation.what: Plain language: electrophoresis spreads serum proteins out by charge into five zones; one cancerous clone of plasma cells shows up as a sharp spike. Scientific terms: zones from anode to cathode are albumin, α1 (α1-antitrypsin), α2 (haptoglobin, α2-macroglobulin, ceruloplasmin), β (transferrin, β-lipoprotein, C3) and γ (immunoglobulins); a homogeneous spike in the γ zone indicates a monoclonal gammopathy, a broad diffuse band a polyclonal gammopathy.
explanation.why: A single clone secretes identical immunoglobulin molecules that migrate together; reactive processes stimulate many clones whose products differ, spreading across the zone. Plasma contains fibrinogen, which forms a narrow band between β and γ that can mimic an M-protein.
explanation.measure: SPEP screens and quantifies; immunofixation (IFE, ~10× more sensitive) identifies heavy and light chains and is required at diagnosis; serum free light chains detect light-chain-only disease; the myeloma work-up includes SPEP with IFE, SFLC and a 24-h urine.
explanation.differs: Monoclonal (narrow spike, IFE shows one heavy + one light chain) vs polyclonal (broad rise; inflammation, infection, cirrhosis); true M-protein vs fibrinogen pseudo-spike (plasma sample, IFE negative).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: fraction order and proteins, spike vs broad rise, the next test after a spike (IFE), light-chain myeloma missed by SPEP, and the plasma/fibrinogen trap.

comparisons.title: Monoclonal vs polyclonal

left.label: Monoclonal
points: One clone; background γ often low
IFE: one heavy + one light chain

comparisons.distinguisher: Width of the γ abnormality and IFE result.

right.label: Plasma
points: Pseudo-spike between β and γ, IFE negative

mnemonic.explanation: Many clones singing slightly different notes give a broad polyclonal hum; one soloist (a single clone) gives a sharp monoclonal spike, and the choir often goes quiet.
mnemonic.limitation: M-proteins can migrate outside γ, small ones can be invisible, light chains may appear mainly in urine, and pseudo-spikes such as fibrinogen exist; immunofixation decides.

analogyLimitations: The choir is a memory device.
Bars stand in for densitometry peaks; heights are not to scale.
The IgG κ result is an invented example.
takeaway: Serum protein electrophoresis screens for monoclonal gammopathies: a narrow spike suggests one clone, a broad rise suggests a reactive polyclonal response, and immunofixation on serum confirms and types the protein.

questions.stem: An SPEP shows a narrow, tall band in the γ region with reduced surrounding γ globulin. What is the best next test?

options.rationale: Correct. IFE confirms a monoclonal protein and identifies its heavy and light chains.

options.text: Repeat SPEP in one year without further testing
options.rationale: Incorrect. A suspected M-protein should be confirmed and typed now.
Incorrect. Haptoglobin evaluates hemolysis, not a γ spike.
Incorrect. That relates to the α1 zone, not the γ spike.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a broad, diffuse increase across the γ region. What does this most likely represent?

options.rationale: Correct. Many clones respond, giving a broad rise; cirrhosis is a classic cause.
Incorrect. A monoclonal protein forms a narrow spike, not a broad rise.
Incorrect. That reduces the α1 band.
Incorrect. Fibrinogen gives a narrow band between β and γ when plasma is used.

questions.stem: A narrow band appears between the β and γ regions; immunofixation is negative. The sample was collected in a lithium heparin tube. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Fibrinogen in plasma creating a pseudo-spike
options.rationale: Correct. Plasma contains fibrinogen, which mimics an M-protein; repeat on serum.
Incorrect. A true M-protein would show on immunofixation.
Incorrect. Polyclonal increases are broad, not narrow.
Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome does not create a narrow β–γ band.
